newsitem.title: JAPAN: POLL-JAPAN JULY TRADE SURPLUS SEEN UP 83 PCT YR/YR.
newsitem.headline: POLL-JAPAN JULY TRADE SURPLUS SEEN UP 83 PCT YR/YR.

text.p: Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus is expected to have recorded another hefty jump in July, with a Reuters poll of economists producing an average forecast of an 83 percent rise from a year ago.
Forecasts ranged from a 60 percent to a 114 percent increase in the surplus, or a surplus of 799 billion yen to 1.07 trillion yen.
The Ministry of Finance will release the customs-cleared trade data at 8.50 a.m. on Monday (2350 GMT Sunday).

Booming exports, particularly in the car sector, combined with weak demand for imports following an increase in the national consumption tax on April 1 continued to push up the surplus in July, economists said.
The poll of economists at 13 financial institutions was conducted on Tuesday.
"Its pretty much the same story as last month, exports are are showing strong growth but imports are only rising a little bit," said Osamu Katano, an economist at Nikko Research.

The wide range in forecasts can be mainly accounted for by the differences in views on how strong exports would be, with those at the high end of the range predicting soaring exports of cars and electronic goods.
Most agreed that domestic demand, still recuperating from pre-tax rise consumer spending sprees. has yet to get back on its feet again although they predicted a tentative recovery from August.
Peter Morgan at HSBC James Capel, pointing to a 0.8 percent fall in imports shown in data for the first 20 days of July, said it was possible imports could be negative for the whole month.
"While I don't think it will be as bad as all that, if it does happen it will be the first time in about three years," he said.
In the first 20 days of July, Japan's trade surplus rose 126 percent, with exports rising 11 percent.
But economists said that while the surplus was on an increasing trend, rises in the July-to-September quarter would not match those in the April-to-June period.
